How to read this page

This is a draft mock-up to support review. It is generated from the project files and rebuilt at each gate. Stated evidence (what a source says, quoted word for word with its item ID) is kept apart from assessed judgements (what the analysis concludes), which appear only from gate G6.

Evidence shown today comes from the extraction sample: 4988 items from 126 of the registered sources. Full extraction follows gates G3 and G4, so counts and examples will change.

Known evidence gaps

  • LIM-0012: English primary; Macedonian or Albanian only for core relevant sources with no suitable English version; each such source recorded in the register; machine translation flagged and capped at Medium confidence
  • LIM-0014: No National Programme for the Adoption of the Acquis (2020 or later) or its implementation reports: the Secretariat for European Affairs site had an expired TLS certificate and no copy was found elsewhere
  • LIM-0015: No official national material on the European Health Insurance Card or the electronic exchange of social security information (EESSI): the Health Insurance Fund site blocks automated access
  • LIM-0016: Documents blocked by publishers for automated download are not retrieved manually in the alpha: SIGMA 2021 and 2024, OECD Competitiveness Outlook 2024 and Labour Migration 2022, UNDP Digital Readiness Assessment, IOM migration profile, two Metamorphosis monitoring reports, the 16th SA Council press statement, State Audit Office originals (ministry copies used)
  • LIM-0017: Research and civil society coverage of Chapter 2 is thin: one think tank study (MKD-RES-2023-001), evaluation highlights only (MKD-RES-2026-001) and one human rights report (MKD-CSO-2024-001)
  • LIM-0018: Almost all national government sources are in Macedonian only (some bilingual with Albanian); evidence on the country response will mostly rely on machine translation capped at Medium confidence
  • LIM-0025: About one in eight in-scope claims may be missed in EU sources, mostly of low importance (37 against 272 items in four sampled sources; the 8 of higher importance added). Long action plans and laws were screened by keyword and section, not read line by line
  • LIM-0028: Comparator evidence uses public sources only. Restricted EU documents are not used, including the EU common position on Montenegro Chapter 2 (AD 26/26), so what closed that benchmark is known only from public statements. Blocked sources, including the SIGMA 2024 reports, are recorded as gaps and not retrieved manually
  • LIM-0029: Comparator legal texts in Croatian, Serbian, Montenegrin or Romanian may be used where no English version exists; they are machine-translated and capped at Medium confidence

IDIssueDefinitionChaptersThemesStatus
RI-FMW-001Nationality discrimination in access to employmentThe law governing access to the labour market does not give EU workers equal treatment with nationals, for example by treating them as any other foreigner or reserving private sector posts for nationals.02Validated
RI-FMW-002Work permits, quotas and residence conditions applied to EU workersEU workers and their family members are subject to work permits, annual quotas, residence permits or unspecified conditions (for example for seasonal work) that must be lifted or settled by accession.02Validated
RI-FMW-003Public sector posts closed to EU citizens beyond the public authority exceptionEU citizens are barred from public sector posts other than a short list of exemptions, rather than only from posts involving the exercise of public authority and safeguarding the general interests of the State.02Validated
RI-FMW-004Legal and organisational framework for joining EURESThe country has not set up the legal and organisational arrangements needed to join the European network of employment services, such as a system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies.02Validated
RI-FMW-005Employment service capacity for EURES and labour mobilityThe public employment service lacks trained staff or adequate IT and data systems to take part in EU labour mobility networks and vacancy exchange.02TECH-INTEROPValidated
RI-FMW-006Alignment with the European Labour Authority regulationNational law is not aligned with the regulation establishing the European Labour Authority, including the arrangements for cooperating with it.02Validated
RI-FMW-007Information and support for mobile workers on their rightsThere is no designated body supporting EU mobile workers in their rights and the system for informing them of their rights is weak.02Validated
RI-FMW-008Gaps in bilateral social security and healthcare agreementsBilateral social security coordination and healthcare agreements do not yet cover all EU Member States or all branches, so workers moving before accession lack coordinated protection.02Validated
RI-FMW-009National social security law not aligned with the coordination regulationsNational pension, health and other social security laws are only partly aligned with the EU coordination regulations, for example through citizenship conditions, and the administrative measures for applying them at accession are not identified or in place.02Validated
RI-FMW-010Readiness for electronic exchange of social security informationThe institutions lack the IT and human capacity to exchange social security information electronically with Member States (the EESSI system) and to use electronic health insurance data.02TECH-INTEROP;TECH-DATAValidated
RI-FMW-011Access to healthcare for EU citizens through the European Health Insurance CardEU citizens can use the European Health Insurance Card or access medical services only where a bilateral arrangement exists, so access is not yet available to citizens of all Member States.02Validated
RI-FMW-012Supplementary pension rights of mobile workersNational law is not aligned with the EU directives on supplementary pension rights, such as the acquisition and preservation of rights for workers who move between Member States.02Validated
RI-FMW-013Weak corruption prevention in the administration of worker mobilityThe bodies administering free movement of workers, notably the employment service, lack a specific integrity policy, internal controls and audit capacity to prevent corruption.02Validated
RI-TEC-001Artificial intelligence framework not aligned or supported by structuresThe rules on artificial intelligence are not aligned with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, or the enforcement structures and wider capacity needed to apply them and support trustworthy uptake are not in place.10TECH-AIValidated
RI-TEC-002Digital transformation strategy and governance weakThere is no adopted long-term strategy for digital transformation aligned with EU targets, or the ministry or agency responsible lacks the capacity, staff and inter-institutional coordination to lead and monitor it.10TECH-DIGI;TECH-DGOVValidated

RI-FMW-001@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentSub-area wording on access to the labour market, which matches this issue, says no progress in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 report says there were no legislative developments. The 2025 screening finding of partial alignment is a first assessment of that kind and does not show a change.Validated
RI-FMW-001@MKDunresolved_gapopenWhat remains is equal treatment of EU workers in the law on access to the labour market, including an end to posts in private companies reserved for nationals. The foreigners law is itself the barrier, the 2025 amendment only renames bodies and the further amendments are only proposed with unknown content (all statuses are proposals; the two government items are machine translated, so capped at Medium), while the country's general ban on nationality discrimination is its own account and does not close the gap. The Commission's statement that the law makes no EU distinction conflicts with the country's account on quotas, which is reported and partly explained under RI-FMW-002.Validated
RI-FMW-001@MKDpriorityHighA key recommendation on non-discrimination against EU workers is repeated in the 2020 to 2025 reports, and equal access is central to the chapter. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found in the evidence.Validated
RI-FMW-001@MKDtractabilityMediumThe change is legal and within the government's control, and the same law was amended in 2021 and 2025. Against that, six reports record no alignment and the requirement runs to the time of accession, so there is no evidence of past progress.Validated
RI-FMW-002@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches; Commission items describe annual quotas and work permits unchanged from 2020 to 2025, and the 2025 seasonal work law leaves conditions for EU citizens to be specified. Permit counts (755 in 2021, some 8 900 in 2024) are not used as a trend, because the bases appear to differ: the 2021 figure sits beside 3 242 separate opinions in a machine-translated agency report, capped at Medium.Validated
RI-FMW-002@MKDunresolved_gapopenWhat remains is access for EU citizens without work permits or residence permits, with their explicit exclusion from quotas, and no responding intervention is linked (statuses are proposals). The confirmed contradiction stands: the Commission says the law does not distinguish EU citizens, while the country says quotas do not apply to them under a reciprocity agreement. Art. 5(2) point 1 of the 2015 law (machine translated, so capped at Medium, and used under LIM-0024) partly explains this, because it does exempt foreigners given equality under such an agreement, but it is conditional, no item identifies a concluded agreement or shows it applied, and the Commission still requires the exclusion.Validated
RI-FMW-002@MKDpriorityMediumPermits and quotas are central to the chapter, but they are named as requirements only in the 2024 report and the screening report, not in the annual key recommendation, which is why this is central with thin support. If the reviewers read the key recommendation on non-discrimination as covering permits and quotas, this would be High; the large item count is mostly the law's own text and did not count.Validated
RI-FMW-002@MKDtractabilityMediumThe change needs only national law, but it involves two laws and the interior and labour ministries and the Employment Agency, and an international organisation reports overlapping mandates between the laws. The law was amended in 2021 and 2025 without touching this requirement, and the proposed amendments have unknown content.Validated
RI-FMW-003@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches. The finding that EU citizens cannot take public administration posts, apart from some in health and education, is unchanged in each report from 2020 to 2025.Validated
RI-FMW-003@MKDunresolved_gapopenWhat remains is limiting the restriction to posts involving public authority and the general interest of the State, in line with case law of the Court of Justice. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare, and the existing exemptions for health and higher education are the country's account and are narrower than the requirement.Validated
RI-FMW-003@MKDpriorityMediumThis is a repeated finding central to the chapter, but public sector posts are named as a requirement only in the screening report and not in an annual key recommendation. If the reviewers read 'in all sectors' in the 2023 to 2025 key recommendation as covering them, this would be High.Validated
RI-FMW-003@MKDtractabilityMediumThe work is national and depends on no outside party, but it requires a careful review of civil servant categories across the public service against case law. There is no evidence of past progress and no responding intervention.Validated
RI-FMW-004@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentSub-area wording on EURES, which matches this issue, says no developments or measures in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and the 2023 key recommendation still asks for alignment. RI-FMW-004@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedWhat remains is a legal system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies. RI-FMW-004@MKDtractabilityMediumOne lead body is planned and the IT and structural base is credited, which helps. However, no legal step has been reported in six years, the country's own timetable runs to 2030 and implementation is tied to accession.Validated
RI-FMW-005@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was context only. RI-FMW-005@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedWhat remains is updated EURES training after staff turnover, with connection of private employment agencies and later ESCO mapping. RI-FMW-006@MKDpriorityMediumThe authority is named in a key recommendation in three reports, but only as part of a sentence mainly about the employment service. The direct support is one source and the issue is not central to the chapter.Validated

RI-TEC-001@MKDdirection_of_travelnewThe EU requirement first appears in 2025 (AI Act alignment and enforcement structures) and the only later EU item, in 2026, concerns the AI Factory Antenna, so there is no repeated EU wording to compare; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. RI-TEC-001@MKDunresolved_gapopenAgainst the single EU alignment ask of 2025, the responding AI legislation and AI strategy are still proposed, and the adopted ICT strategy and signed Antenna grant do not supply alignment or enforcement; these statuses are themselves proposals. RI-TEC-001@MKDpriorityMediumThe rating rests only on the EU layer: one body-text invitation in the 2025 report to align fully with the AI Act, plus a 2026 readout that encourages outreach and does not mention the Act. The much larger national audit, strategy and research evidence (over 200 of 229 items, mostly from a few documents) describes the gap but was given no weight here.Validated
RI-TEC-001@MKDtractabilityMediumDrafting is within government control, with the EU Act as a template and AI legislation already listed in an adopted action plan, but enforcement structures need a designated authority, specialist staff and funding, across several bodies. RI-TEC-002@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe only movement is that the key recommendation to finalise and adopt the ICT strategy, unchanged from 2020 to 2024, ended in 2025 because the strategy was adopted, and adoption is not improvement in governance. RI-TEC-002@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe latest EU items report the strategy adopted but still ask for stronger ministry capacity, more IT staff and the digital agency, which remains proposed and which the country has said it will reassess; these statuses are themselves proposals, and that of the National Council is unclear because the 2024 audit found no 2023 activity while the strategy cites its formation. The Commission's well-structured set-up and the national vacuum are a noted difference of scope, not a conflict.Validated
RI-TEC-002@MKDpriorityHighThe ICT strategy was a Chapter 10 key recommendation in five successive reports, and the ministry capacity ask has recurred in four reports to 2025, on an issue central to the digital transformation theme. National plans and audits were not counted towards this rating.Validated
RI-TEC-002@MKDtractabilityMediumA new ministry and an adopted strategy show that institutional steps can be taken, but the strategy took over five years and coordination depends on many institutions that have offered limited cooperation. RI-TEC-004@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe change since the Commission's 2023 call for basic systems is the adoption of the electronic archiving law in 2025 and the Reform Agenda steps themselves, and adoption alone does not show improvement. RI-TEC-004@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedOf the three Reform Agenda requirements, the law is adopted and the Commission treats that step as achieved, but it applied only from June 2026 with by-laws still proposed, the e-platform is proposed and the document system is only partially operational; these statuses are themselves proposals. RI-TEC-004@MKDpriorityHighThe archiving law, the storage platform and the single document system are named Reform Agenda steps with payments attached, and these shared systems are central to the digital government theme.
