RI-TEC-004@MKDtractabilityMediumThe tasks are bounded, led by one ministry and backed by payment incentives, and the legal step was achieved by its 2025 deadline. Roll-out is harder: it needs hardware, licences, training and change of working habits in many institutions, and earlier piloting left 22 institutions using a small part of the system. The national evidence on use is machine translated and capped at Medium.Validated
RI-TEC-033@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission's wording is close to unchanged across reports: advancing but low in 2020 to 2023, advancing slowly in 2024 and 2025, and low in 2026, with one 2025 note that SME adoption has accelerated but stays uneven and basic. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 54.5% website figure repeats across reports and was not treated as new evidence, and the 3% and 19.7% online sales figures use different populations, so they show no trend.Validated
RI-TEC-033@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe latest EU asks concern support to companies through the innovation hub and active use of Digital Europe calls; the hub is set up and the association agreement signed, while vouchers, the support portal and the grant mechanism are proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is actual use of these channels and SME adoption beyond basic technologies, as the Commission still reported low digitalisation in 2026.Validated
RI-TEC-033@MKDpriorityMediumThe finding is repeated in most years, largely in economic governance documents, but it has few specific recommendations; the only key recommendation found is the 2025 hub item, and no benchmark or payment condition names it in the input. It is therefore a repeated EU concern that is not central to accession steps.Validated
RI-TEC-033@MKDtractabilityMediumGovernment can fund and steer support, and EU programmes and a first hub already exist, but results depend on many small firms' demand, skills and finance. Past effort is small and not evaluated: EUR 0.5 million budgeted in 2023, and the strategy itself says there has been no support mechanism for projects of greater national importance; that source is machine translated and capped at Medium.Validated
RI-TEC-034@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe ask to align with the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act recurs with little change in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and e-commerce was described as slow in 2021, 2022 and 2023. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Growth figures for online transactions are country-reported, partly repeated and on differing bases, so they were not read as closing the issue.Validated
RI-TEC-034@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe latest EU items still require alignment with the DSA, DMA and Geo-blocking Regulation, and the responding alignment measures are all proposed, with national targets of 2027 and 2028 and only training delivered; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is the alignment itself for all these acts, plus full alignment on electronic commerce. The country's report of being largely aligned with the e-Commerce Directive and the Commission's call to align fully differ in degree and speaker, and were not treated as closure.Validated
RI-TEC-034@MKDpriorityMediumThe requirement is repeated in three reports and relates to binding acquis, but it sits in Chapter 10 body text, not in the 2024 or 2025 key recommendations, and is not named as a benchmark or payment condition in the input. It is therefore a repeated EU requirement that is not central under the criteria.Validated
RI-TEC-034@MKDtractabilityMediumThe work is mainly legislative with EU texts as templates, a government timetable and a request for expert group participation, which depends partly on the Commission. No draft is reported and past progress is limited to training, and applying platform rules will need capacity that the input does not evidence.Validated
RI-TEC-035@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe alignment ask on digital tools in company law recurs in near-identical wording in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, so the default applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 2025 screening finding of a high level of alignment shows the remaining ask is narrow, but it is not evidence of change over time.Validated
RI-TEC-035@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedFully online company registration is in practice and the Commission finds high alignment, on a status that is itself a proposal. What remains is further alignment with Directive (EU) 2019/1151, including scrutiny of a company's object and verification of directors' appointment and disqualification. The country's statement that it is aligned and the Commission's statement that further alignment is necessary are a confirmed contradiction, reported here and not resolved.Validated
RI-TEC-035@MKDpriorityMediumIt appears in the key recommendations of three reports, but always bundled with other company law items, and digital tools are a narrow strand on which the Commission already finds high alignment. It is therefore a repeated EU requirement that is not central to the chapter, and it is not a benchmark or payment condition in the input.Validated
RI-TEC-035@MKDtractabilityHighThe remaining points are specific legal amendments in a field with few actors and a working one-stop-shop registry, and they depend on no other institution's roll-out. The ask has nonetheless stood since 2021 with no reported draft, which is why the rating depends on the small scope and not on past momentum.Validated
RI-TEC-005@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission's recommendation to keep extending taxpayer e-services recurs every year from 2020 to 2026 with almost no change, moving only from 'further extend' to 'continue the process of expansion', so the default applies; this is one repeated view, not independent evidence. The Chapter 16 'Some progress' wording of 2021 is context only and was not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-005@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe Commission still asks in 2026 for expansion, while e-Tax, e-VAT and pre-filled returns are proposed as in practice and the electronic tax administration only as proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the Macedonian-language plan items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. What remains is a wider range of taxpayer e-services, with the electronic tax administration still at project documentation and draft legislation stage.Validated
RI-TEC-005@MKDpriorityMediumThe recommendation is repeated across more than three reports, but taxpayer e-services are one clause beside business processes, the integrated IT system and compliance risk, so the issue is not central to Chapter 16 or the theme. The Reform Agenda's e-services step names the fiscal sector only as an example, and this was not read as a payment condition on this issue.Validated
RI-TEC-005@MKDtractabilityHighOne agency leads, working platforms exist, and upgrades are reported by the Commission, so progress depends little on other actors or the EU. A caution is that the source does not say how far further e-services depend on the integrated IT system, which has been outstanding since 2020.Validated
RI-TEC-006@MKDdirection_of_travelimprovingThe e-market moved from development in 2021 to launch in 2022, and awards rose from 70 in 2022 to 258 in 2023 (259 in the Reform Agenda, a minor difference of count), with 350 small-value transactions in 2024, though that item does not name the e-market. The Commission's finding of poor use in 2023 is not repeated later, and no later item shows change on e-catalogues or red-flag analysis. The Chapter 5 'Limited progress' wording of 2022 and 2025 is context only and was not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-006@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe system is working and the e-market and red-flag modules are proposed as in practice, with the low-value bylaw at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is raising e-market use from 350 to the required 800 awards in 2026, wider take-up of e-catalogues, and the data analysis the Commission asked for in 2023.Validated
RI-TEC-006@MKDpriorityMediumE-market use is a Reform Agenda payment condition, which meets one limb of the High test, but the Commission finds the core system functions efficiently and the shortfall concerns low-value contracts and add-on modules. It is therefore not central to Chapter 5 or the theme, and the proposal rests on that reading of centrality.Validated
RI-TEC-006@MKDtractabilityHighOne bureau runs a platform that is already obligatory for all contracting authorities, awards rose about fivefold in two years, and a payment is attached to the target. The main limit is the confidence of contracting authorities, and the target is still more than double the 2024 count.Validated
RI-TEC-007@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe requirement that the point of single contact be upgraded to meet the Services Directive is unchanged in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the register of regulated professions moves from unfinished data validation (2020, 2021) to 'yet to be put in place' (2024, 2025). The contact point itself did advance, from early stage in 2021 to a platform with 312 online services in 2025, so the two limbs of this issue point different ways. No Chapter 3 scale rating is linked to the issue, and the scale would be context only.Validated
RI-TEC-007@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedA contact point platform exists and is proposed as implemented, but the Commission finds it not fully in line with the acquis and the list and register still absent; these statuses are themselves proposals. Sources conflict on which body is the contact point (Central Register or uslugi.gov.mk), and the 238 (2023) and 124 (2024) service counts are not explained. What remains is full online information and procedures under the Services Directive, especially on licences, and a transparent electronic register of all regulated professions.Validated
RI-TEC-007@MKDpriorityMediumThe point of single contact was a key recommendation only in 2021, 2022 and 2023, with the 2021 item flagged as doubtful for the theme, and later Commission items on it and the 2025 item on the register of professions are in body text, so the requirement is repeated. It is a sector portal under the Services Directive and is not central to the digital government theme, which is the same reading applied to taxpayer e-services (RI-TEC-005) and e-procurement (RI-TEC-006). Its importance to Chapter 3 is not the test for a technology issue, and no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition names it.Validated
RI-TEC-007@MKDtractabilityMediumThe platform is in place and service numbers have been added, which favours progress on the contact point. Against that, sectoral laws must be aligned, the responsible body is unclear between sources, and a register of all professions needs input from many regulators.Validated
RI-TEC-009@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentCommission wording on extending Moj Termin is the same in 2022 and 2023, and non-interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data recurs in 2024 and 2025, with non-alignment of legislation added in the 2025 screening. Functional upgrades in 2023 and 2025 are real but have not changed the stated shortfall. The default for three unchanged reports is not strictly triggered, and no Chapter 28 scale rating was decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-009@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe 2025 report still asks for interoperability, and the responding steps are proposed (population register and wallet connections) or at insufficient evidence (platform for traceability), none naming Health Insurance Fund data; these statuses are themselves proposals and the plan items are machine translated, capped at Medium confidence. The paper-referral finding and the screening's account of a tool holding referrals are a noted difference, not a conflict, since storing data and issuing on paper can both be true, but practice needs checking. What remains is interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data, an end to paper referrals, and alignment with the eHealth acquis.Validated
RI-TEC-009@MKDpriorityMediumThe Commission's requirement is repeated in 2024 and 2025 and raised to a recommendation in 2025, but it is a narrow part of Chapter 28 and only recently prominent. The Reform Agenda's e-services step names the health sector as an example, and this was not read as a payment condition on this issue.Validated
RI-TEC-009@MKDtractabilityMediumA central tool and one lead ministry exist and upgrades are reported, but interoperability needs the Health Insurance Fund as well, and alignment with the acquis needs legislation. National plan and World Bank items add that the platform needs upgrading and users need digital literacy; the plan item is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-010@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentCommission calls for digital court communication and connected IT recur in 2020, 2023, 2024 and 2025, with identical wording in the last two, and the single 2026 item on the administrative courts cannot alone show a change of direction. Support is thin (eight items, none for 2021 or 2022, most flagged theme_doubtful), and no chapter scale was decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-010@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe administrative courts' interconnection is proposed as implemented and the Commission calls it a key advancement, but no status is recorded for the judicial IT strategies and council, and Luris is at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is digital communication with courts generally, videoconferencing for hearings, and connections between other justice institutions, including the Ministry of Justice and the prosecution.Validated
RI-TEC-010@MKDpriorityMediumThe recommendation is repeated, including in the 2024 and 2025 reports, within the important Chapter 23 area, but digital communication is a supporting part of judicial reform and no benchmark or payment condition on it appears in the input. Evidence is thin and most items are flagged theme_doubtful.Validated
RI-TEC-010@MKDtractabilityMediumOne interconnection shows that progress is possible, but several independent justice institutions must act together, and the Commission points to weak coordination. The evidence on actors and resources is thin, so this rating is tentative.Validated
RI-TEC-036@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentFrom 2020 to 2026 the Commission repeats the same shortfall: too few fully transactional services, low use and below-expectation results, ending with 'quite underdeveloped' in 2026, and the world index rank falls from 72 to 80 to 84 (the last from a machine-translated strategy table, capped at Medium confidence). The 2025 report does record a real change, with most-demanded services and some certificates now online, so the case for 'improving' is open but rests on one report that the 2026 finding does not bear out. The Chapter 10 scale (Some, Limited, Limited, Some progress in 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and service counts were not used for trend because their definitions differ.Validated
RI-TEC-036@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe portal is proposed as in practice and its upgrade as implemented, while the Reform Agenda reform is proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the upgrade status sits uneasily with the Commission's 2024 note that the 135 services were not yet configured. Progress against the 50% target cannot be fixed, because the 264 baseline conflicts with the Commission's 392 and 124 figures, and 246 also conflicts with 124, so sources are cited both ways. What remains is a much wider set of fully transactional, commonly requested services that people actually use, on an agreed count, and equal access, where the Commission's statement that the portal caters for special needs conflicts with the audit's finding (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services.Validated
RI-TEC-036@MKDpriorityHighThe e-services increase is a Reform Agenda payment condition, and widening the portal's services is a recommendation repeated across three or more reports, including 'treat as a priority' in the 2025 screening. It is central to the digital government theme and Chapter 10. The rating rests on these, not on the large number of national audit and strategy items.Validated
RI-TEC-036@MKDtractabilityMediumA single platform, EU funding and a dated payment step favour progress, and the Commission reports new services in 2025. Against that, the Commission's own wording shows the 135-service upgrade slipping for years and fragmented ownership, and the State Audit Office (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) reports about 140 laws unaligned and 101 of 242 posts unfilled, which means many institutions must act.Validated
RI-TEC-037@MKDdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceNo repeated Commission wording or comparable series exists: EU items are isolated additions (2024, 2025), and the Chapter 10 scale is context only and was not decisive. The other signals are partial and mixed, since e-Rabota's share of employer registrations rose from 60% to 69% but fell from 67% to 62% for agencies in government reports, and a civil society study finds general slow progress at municipal level. Government and civil society items here are Low or Medium confidence, and the Macedonian ones are machine translated.Validated
RI-TEC-037@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedSector services exist, and One Stop Shops are proposed as implemented, while the analysis on e-services there, the mobile offices and the employment plan are proposed or at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the national items are machine translated, capped at Medium confidence. The Commission's requirement is general, not specific. What remains is a wider range and use of sector and local services, including municipal ones, with published statistics on delivery.Validated
RI-TEC-037@MKDpriorityLowThe Commission mentions sector services only briefly, and most of the concern is raised by the national audit (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence), national plans and civil society, so the issue meets the test of being mainly raised by others. The Reform Agenda target falls on the national portal under the G5 split, and item volume was not counted.Validated
RI-TEC-037@MKDtractabilityMediumIndividual sector bodies can and do make progress, as e-Rabota and the Cadastre Office show. Across many institutions and municipalities, however, the audit and ICT strategy (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) describe parallel systems built without clear guidance, and no single actor has control.Validated
RI-TEC-011@MKDdirection_of_travelimprovingCommission wording that the law needs further alignment repeated from 2020 to 2022, and the matching sub-area wording in 2023 was no progress, but the wording then changed: the 2025 assessment found significant gaps after the new law, and the 2026 assessment found alignment partially achieved after the December 2025 amendments. The chapter-wide limited progress of 2024 is context only and was not decisive. Sources conflict on the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive: the Commission said in 2024 that the country was yet to align, while the country's reported view in the screening is full alignment, and this is not resolved here.Validated
RI-TEC-011@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe Commission's May 2026 assessment considers the Reform Agenda step not achieved and the beneficiary considers it achieved, as it did in 2025, so the two sides conflict and the Commission's finding is the requirement compared here. Responding interventions carry proposed statuses that the reviewers check at G6: the 2025 law and December amendments adopted, the by-laws and 2026 draft amendments only proposed, and the law applicable only from 1 June 2026, with no evidence on the outcome of the grace period ending 30 June 2026. What remains is closing the harmonisation gaps with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act in both laws and adopting and applying the by-laws; the ePrivacy conflict is left to its own issue under the taxonomy.Validated
RI-TEC-011@MKDpriorityHighAdoption of an aligned law is a Reform Agenda step with a payment provision, and alignment with the Code recurs in the Commission's chapter recommendations from 2022 to 2025. It is central to the digital infrastructure theme because other reforms in the area rest on this legal framework. The roaming and net neutrality parts of the issue are largely positive and do not drive this rating.Validated
RI-TEC-011@MKDtractabilityMediumThe mechanisms are legal alignment and implementing rules, led by one ministry with the regulator and parliament, and a new law and amendments were adopted in 2025, which favours progress. Against that, the Commission assessed the Reform Agenda step as not achieved in both 2025 and 2026, with gaps remaining in two laws, and the by-laws are described as technically demanding and were not yet due. Adoption has been quick but alignment has twice fallen short, which does not support High.Validated
RI-TEC-012@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentCommission concern about the regulator's independence recurs in nearly unchanged terms in each report from 2020 to 2025, with no recorded improvement, so the default applies; in September 2024 parliament dismissed all five commission members, which the source reports without saying what it meant for independence. The chapter scale was not decisive. The competition part has moved a little, from no relevant developments in 2020 and 2021 to a market still shared by two operators in 2023 and a new operator taking part in a frequency tender in 2025, so the two parts of this issue do not move together.Validated
RI-TEC-012@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe latest Commission items still ask for the regulator's independence to be ensured and bolstered, and the 2025 law's statement that the Agency is independent is a legal provision, not evidence of practice. The compared statuses are proposals for G6: the law is adopted, while the third operator and the frequency tender are only proposed, and the latest evidence on the tender is a sole bidder with a decision deadline of 12 January 2026, in machine-translated regulator reporting. What remains is independence shown in appointments and practice, more competition in a concentrated mobile market, and resolving the financing provisions for the Operational and Technical Agency, on which the Commission and the country disagree and which concern that agency and not the regulator itself.Validated
RI-TEC-012@MKDpriorityHighStrengthening the independence and capacity of this regulator is a key Commission recommendation repeated in every report from 2021 to 2025, and an independent regulator is central to the digital infrastructure theme. It is not itself a Reform Agenda step, and the recommendation is shared with the media regulators, which are outside this issue. The rating rests on the independence part; the competition part is supported by repeated but less prominent findings.Validated
RI-TEC-012@MKDtractabilityMediumThe two parts differ. Independence looks hard, because it depends on appointments by parliament and exposure to political interests, and six years of reports record no progress, while competition looks more realistic because a tender has reached a compliant bid. That tender rests on one bidder and was held up by elections and a missing opinion from the anti-corruption commission, as machine-translated regulator reporting states, so Medium is a blend that would not hold if the issue were split.Validated
RI-TEC-013@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission's sentence that smaller companies still face obstacles repeats from 2021 to 2026 with the same figures, so the default applies, though repeats are not independent evidence, and in 2025 the wording hardened to significant obstacles for smaller companies and rural areas. National averages did rise, with home internet access at 90.8% in 2024, 5G coverage at 76% in 2023 and 97% in a machine-translated 2025 national source, and some progress on ICT infrastructure in matching sub-area wording in 2025, while differences between earlier household figures reflect different measures, not conflict. No series tracks the rural and small-business gap itself, so the averages do not show that the unevenness has narrowed, and the chapter scale was not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-013@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedLatest EU items still ask for more access for smaller companies and rural areas, while the compared statuses, which are proposals for G6, show 5G roll-out in practice but the national optical network only proposed. Sources conflict on the size of the gap: the ICT strategy gives 77% fixed coverage against an EU average of 78%, the Commission gives 79.6% against 93.1%, and the strategy elsewhere gives 77% as very high capacity coverage after stating 69%, so the comparison with the EU cannot be relied on until the measures are checked. What remains is fixed broadband for small firms and rural areas, very low take-up of the fastest connections, and completing the 5G roll-out named in the Reform Agenda.Validated
RI-TEC-013@MKDpriorityHighRoll-out of 5G network and services is named in a Reform Agenda step, and the Commission repeats the particular need to increase access to broadband in its assessments from 2021 to 2026, which makes it central to the digital infrastructure theme. The payment condition covers the 5G part, not the rural and small-business part, which appears in repeated assessments and not in the chapter's key recommendations. The large volume of items on this issue, much of it repeated wording and national statistics, did not raise the rating.Validated
RI-TEC-013@MKDtractabilityMediumPast progress is clear on 5G and on general access, where operators have invested and the Commission records continued expansion. The harder part depends on resources and on others: rural and low-demand areas lack commercial interest, the national network is at feasibility stage on a timetable to 2030 with mixed financing, and the government's own strategy, in machine translation, names lack of finance and high prices as challenges. Delivery therefore needs the ministry, the public broadcasting enterprise, operators and outside funders.Validated
RI-TEC-014@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe plan's implementation slowed in 2021 and was further delayed in 2022, a strategic approach to broadband was found lacking in 2022 and 2023, the plan was said only to remain valid in 2024 and 2025, and the 2025 screening asks for its targets to be aligned with the Digital Decade; the 2020 chapter-wide some progress is context and was not decisive. Newer Reform Agenda investment and a feasibility study are plans and do not yet show change, so this is not improving, and no 2026 Commission item addresses the framework. Sources conflict on the plan's period, with ITU and the 2025 report giving 2019-2029 and the 2022 and 2024 reports giving 2019-2023, which affects how far the delays can be measured against targets.Validated
RI-TEC-014@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe latest EU items ask for targets aligned with the Digital Decade, further alignment on aid for broadband and stronger capacity at the public broadcasting enterprise. The compared statuses are proposals for G6: the ICT strategy with its 2030 goals is adopted, but its alignment with the Digital Decade is the government's own statement in machine translation, and target alignment, State aid and the national network are only proposed, while none of the three plan measures towards the 100 Mbps target has been implemented. What remains is updating the plan's targets, settling the aid rules and financing the backhaul network; the reported non-use of the Western Balkans Investment Framework for infrastructure sits beside technical assistance from it for a feasibility study, which appears to be a difference between study and construction but should be checked.Validated
RI-TEC-014@MKDpriorityMediumThe requirement is repeated by the EU, in the 2022 and 2023 assessments and the 2025 screening, but it is not named in a benchmark, a Reform Agenda payment step or the chapter's key recommendations. The Reform Agenda plan does call the broadband network the most important digital project, but as an investment, so the issue matters for the theme with thinner support than the legal and regulator issues.Validated
RI-TEC-014@MKDtractabilityMediumUpdating targets is within the government's control and a mapping study is the stated first step, but financing the network depends on outside funders, State aid alignment and a public enterprise whose capacity the Commission says needs strengthening. Past progress is weak: the plan was delayed in 2021 and 2022, and the national broadband competence office, reported in machine translation, finds none of three measures implemented. The financing figures come from a table flagged as possibly misread, so they support only the general point that funding is mixed.Validated
RI-TEC-015@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission repeated the need to improve population register data in 2021, 2022 and 2023, and the same recommendation to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers in 2023, 2024 and 2025, with use of the register still limited in 2024. The 2025 mention of efforts does not change the recommendation, so the default of persistent applies. The Chapter 10 scale is context only and was not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-015@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe population register is proposed as in practice, but the register platform, the Register of Registers and the wider e-services reform are all proposed only, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is to complete the digitalisation of institutional, municipal property and intellectual property registers and to raise the quality and use of population register data. The fully digital National Real Estate Register and the Commission's analogue property registers are a noted difference of register and level, not a conflict, and the machine-translated strategy on low use is capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-015@MKDpriorityHighThe Commission's main findings gave the same key recommendation to complete register digitalisation in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and base registers are central to the digital government theme. The recommendation is one clause of a wider one on administrative procedures and is shared with the data exchange and e-services issues, which reviewers may weigh. The Reform Agenda payment step on a register of charges is flagged as doubtful for this theme and was not relied on.Validated
RI-TEC-015@MKDtractabilityMediumThe operating population register shows that delivery is possible, and a register platform was begun with EU support. Against that, completion needs many institutions and municipalities to act, and the strategy's baseline of no digital registers in 2022 shows how much remains. The two strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-016@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentCommission items ask for regular data updates in 2020 and more proactive disclosure in 2022, while amendments for Open Data Directive alignment were in preparation in 2023 and still with a working group in 2025; the 2020 sub-area rating of some progress concerns transparency more widely and, like the chapter scale, was not decisive. The State Audit Office reports that the portal has not functioned since early 2025, in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and the country's published screening presentation describes the portal favourably without addressing this. That outage rests on one source with no later status, so it does not yet support worsening, though confirmation would.Validated
RI-TEC-016@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedA Law on the Use of Public Sector Data is adopted and 580 datasets were reported by 2022, but the amendments and the Directive alignment action are proposed only, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is alignment with the Open Data Directive and regular publication by institutions on a functioning portal. Sources conflict, since the October 2025 strategy says the country is not aligned while the screening report's country presentation says partially aligned, so both are the country's own statements (the conflict register attributes the second to the Commission), and the Commission's own finding is only that further efforts are needed; the machine-translated items are capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-016@MKDpriorityMediumThe Commission raises the matter in 2020, 2022 and 2025, but not in its main findings, so it is a repeated requirement that is not central. Most items here come from one national audit and one national strategy, and that volume was not treated as importance.Validated
RI-TEC-016@MKDtractabilityHighOne ministry leads, the portal and 74 publishing institutions already existed by 2022, and the stated cause of the outage is a procurement problem rather than a structural one. Progress does not depend on the EU, although the amendments have been slow since 2023. This view leans on machine-translated items capped at Medium confidence, and government reporting on datasets does not itself show success.Validated
RI-TEC-017@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission found no concrete progress on the Law Enforcement Directive in 2020, partial alignment and a need for full alignment in 2023, and pending alignment in 2024 and 2025, so the requirement has not changed across three or more reports. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2024 and 2025 covers more than this issue and was not decisive. The 2025 transfer amendment without equivalent safeguards is a further concern but a single event.Validated
RI-TEC-017@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe 2020 law is proposed as in practice, with the Commission confirming full application from August 2021, while the amendments and the Law Enforcement Directive law are proposed only, the earlier draft was withdrawn in 2022, and all these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is full alignment with the General Data Protection Regulation, a law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, safeguards for transfers, harmonised sector laws and confirmed ePrivacy alignment. Sources conflict, since the State Audit Office and the Agency's strategy describe the law as aligned while the Commission calls the framework insufficient, and the country claims full ePrivacy alignment while the Commission seeks further efforts; this judgement does not rely on Article 122 of the unofficial translation (MKD-GOV-2020-001-0043), which may be mistranslated and, read literally, would suspend core chapters until accession.Validated
RI-TEC-017@MKDpriorityHighFull alignment with the data protection rules is central to the data theme and is repeated by the Commission in 2023, 2024 and 2025, but none of the 2020 to 2025 reports names it in the key recommendations, and it is in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition. The 2024 and 2025 main findings record no progress, but that is a finding and not a key recommendation, so this is a central requirement with thin support under the test. National and agency items were not counted.Validated overridden
RI-TEC-017@MKDtractabilityMediumTexts already exist: the Agency drafted amendments in April 2022 and a Law Enforcement Directive draft reached Parliament with, as the Agency reports, a positive informal Commission opinion. Yet the Government withdrew that draft in 2022, neither process moved in 2025, and sector laws need several ministries. The Agency's annual report items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-018@MKDdirection_of_travelworseningThe Commission moved from dependence on ministries in 2021 and understaffing in 2022 and 2023 to staff falling further in 2024 and no director in 2025, with reported staff of 21, then 20, then 18 at the end of 2024 and 17 at the end of 2025. The last two counts are the Agency's own, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, but they run the same way as the Commission's findings. The Agency reports a director from 5 December 2025, which is a later date than the Commission's finding, not a conflict, and the chapter scale was not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-018@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe amendments meant to secure the Agency's autonomy are proposed only, and the 2025-2030 strategy's proposed status of implemented means only that work has begun, with the Commission finding it was held back; these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is autonomy in hiring and spending, and funding and staff that match the Agency's tasks. Statements that the Agency is independent describe its legal status, while the Commission and the Agency's own reports describe its operating dependence, so this is a noted difference and not a conflict.Validated
RI-TEC-018@MKDpriorityMediumThe Commission has raised the Agency's dependence and capacity from 2021 to 2025 and an independent authority is central to the data theme, but the requirement appears only in body text, in 2023 and 2025 and in the 2025 communication in general terms. It is in no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, and the main findings do not mention it, so it is a central requirement with thin support, on the same footing as RI-TEC-019.Validated
RI-TEC-018@MKDtractabilityMediumOnly a few domestic actors are needed, a draft has existed since April 2022 and the budget is small. Past progress is poor, however: the draft has not moved, the Ministry of Finance repeatedly refused funds or returned the employment plan, and the director post took most of 2025 to fill. The Agency's reports are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and they are a party's account of its own constraints.Validated
RI-TEC-019@MKDdirection_of_travelworseningThe Commission's finding was essentially unchanged from 2020 to 2024, with some progress noted in 2021, and then changed in 2025, when the Government removed the Agency from the mandatory consultation list and Parliament amended the law without consulting it. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2025 matches this issue and the chapter scale was not decisive. The Agency's report confirms the deletion in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and its count of opinions (5 for 2024, 15 for 2025) does not show that consultation improved.Validated
RI-TEC-019@MKDunresolved_gapopenNo intervention is recorded as responding to this issue, and the one recent measure, the removal from the consultation list, has a proposed status of implemented and runs the opposite way; these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is systematic consultation of the Agency on sector and implementing laws, follow-up of its recommendations and follow-up of its reports in Parliament.Validated
RI-TEC-019@MKDpriorityMediumThe finding recurs in every report from 2020 to 2025 and the Commission called the 2025 removal concerning, but the 2023 list of areas requiring alignment does not include it and it is not in the main findings. It is a repeated requirement that supports the authority's role rather than being central to the theme, and reviewers may weigh the 2025 reversal differently.Validated
RI-TEC-019@MKDtractabilityMediumRestoring the consultation duty is a change to the Government's own Rules of Procedure, which the Agency identifies precisely and which depends on no one outside the country. Getting ministries to follow advice and Parliament to act on reports is harder, and the Government removed the duty recently. The Agency's items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-020@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission called fines low in 2020, found in general that controllers do not implement the law in 2023, and in 2025 found low awareness and more frequent breaches, some unreported; the 2022 statement of progress on compliance sits in the paragraph on one body's supervision, so it is not a general trend. The Agency's statements of significant progress concern its own application of the framework, a noted difference from the Commission's sub-area rating, and supervision counts measure enforcement rather than compliance. The chapter scale was not decisive, and the machine-translated Agency findings are capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-020@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe security rulebook has been adopted and the e-classroom is proposed as implemented, but the data protection officer network and the sanction amendments are proposed only, no independent evidence shows changed behaviour, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is for controllers, including public bodies, to apply the law, report breaches and face effective sanctions. Reprimand counts conflict between the Commission's report (10 for 2022, 17 for 2021) and the country presentation (4 for each), and low notification numbers (19 for 2022, 11 for 2025) are read by the Agency as under-reporting, so they do not conflict with the Commission's finding of more frequent breaches.Validated
RI-TEC-020@MKDpriorityMediumCompliance is central to whether the law has effect, but the Commission's direct findings on it are thin, mainly 2023 and 2025, and it is not a named key recommendation. The large volume of items comes from the Agency's own reports and was not treated as importance.Validated
RI-TEC-020@MKDtractabilityLowProgress needs behaviour to change across very many public and private controllers, and it depends on an Agency whose supervision and misdemeanour capacity is shrinking. The evidence shows awareness work and enforcement activity, but no sustained improvement in compliance. The Agency's items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-021@MKDdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceThe Commission used the same wording in three documents, its 2022 and 2023 reports and the 2023 screening report, but no item after 2023 addresses the issue, so the record shows neither that it continues nor that it has eased. The three-report default for persistent was therefore not applied, because the repeats span only two years and the 2024 and 2025 reports are silent. The chapter scale was not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-021@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe latest requirement, from 2023, is unmet on the record: no intervention is recorded as responding and the Electoral Code's biometric provisions have a proposed status of adopted, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is an assessment of the Code against data protection law and proper oversight of personal data used in campaigns. The State Election Commission addressed some irregularities, but that does not reach these two points, and this finding rests on evidence no newer than 2023.Validated
RI-TEC-021@MKDpriorityLowThe Commission raised it only in 2022 and 2023, it is not in the main findings, and it is peripheral to the data theme.Validated
RI-TEC-021@MKDtractabilityMediumFew actors are needed and an assessment of the Code is a limited task, and the State Election Commission has already acted on some irregularities. Oversight of campaign data and any change to the Electoral Code are likely to be harder, and the evidence on this is thin.Validated
RI-TEC-022@MKDdirection_of_travelimprovingCommission items moved from no further progress on the 2019 draft law in 2021, through repeated calls to adopt the law and strategy in 2022, 2023 and 2024, to adoption of the strategy in January 2025 and the law in June 2025, which the 2025 report counts as some progress. The chapter scale (limited progress 2021 to 2024, some progress 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and the improvement lies in the legal and strategic framework, since no item shows better coordination after the 2023 call, the 2024 audit finding of a Council that met once and the 2025 strategy's own description of coordination as critical. A February 2022 ITU item lists the law as existing while the Commission's 2022 report says it was still a draft, and later Commission and audit items support the draft reading; the differing dates for the Council (2019 or 2020) and the action plan's end (2027 or 2028) do not affect this value.Validated
RI-TEC-022@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe Commission found the 2025 law sufficient for the Reform Agenda step, which required alignment of primary legislation only, yet says it does not fully align with the acquis and still asks the country to continue aligning; the law, strategy and competent authority are proposed as adopted and the by-laws and disclosure and crisis frameworks as proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is the outstanding NIS2 provisions and Cybersecurity Act certification alignment (last raised before the law passed), the 15 by-laws legally due within six months but not shown as adopted, the entity lists, the disclosure and crisis frameworks, working coordination, and application to the sectors the law defers until accession. The law's text is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and the regulator's one-line statement that the strategy is applied is government reporting without specifics, so neither is treated as closure.Validated
RI-TEC-022@MKDpriorityHighThe law and strategy, an operational competent authority and the NIS2 frameworks are each Reform Agenda payment steps, and NIS2 or cybersecurity legislation recurs in the Commission's key recommendations from 2022 to 2025. The issue is the legal base on which the rest of the cybersecurity theme rests. The rating rests on these EU requirements and not on the large number of national plan and audit items.Validated
RI-TEC-022@MKDtractabilityMediumMuch of what remains is drafting that the Ministry controls, and adoption followed within a year of the Reform Agenda step, which favours progress; against this, the first draft law stalled from 2019 to 2025, the Council barely functioned and no item shows the by-laws adopted after their deadline. Coordination needs many bodies, the strategy itself names political support and budget as key risks, and one reporting obligation to ENISA cannot be met outside the EU. Tractability is therefore higher for legal alignment than for coordination.Validated
RI-TEC-023@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission's wording is essentially unchanged across three reports, that state institutions need stronger capacity and infrastructure and the national centre more staff (2023, 2024, 2025), and its reform programme assessments repeat large or major deficiencies in 2025 and 2026, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Incident counts cannot show a trend in capacity, because reporting was not mandatory and the figures are not comparable (1,441 or 1,443 for 2020, 2,804 for 2022, about 170 in 2023 on an unstated definition). The World Bank's advanced rating and the audit's finding of poor protection are a noted difference and not a conflict, since an index of national commitments and a test of practice measure different things, and the 2024 index itself lists technical and capacity measures as areas for growth.Validated
RI-TEC-023@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe latest EU items, of November 2025 and April 2026, still call for significant strengthening and report major deficiencies, while responses are proposed as adopted on paper (the law, strategy and action plan, the national and government response teams) or only planned (government data centre, secure network, security operations centre), and the disaster recovery centre is used by 3 of about 140 bodies; these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is staffed and trained response teams working to the Reform Agenda standard, security officers and tested plans in institutions, and secure government infrastructure in actual use. The Reform Agenda's 2024 baseline of CERTs not operational sits against statements that MKD-CIRT is in place, possibly because the baseline means NIS2 readiness, and the audit evidence behind this finding is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence, with percentages from a survey of 18 institutions.Validated
RI-TEC-023@MKDpriorityHighOperational national and government CERTs, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network are Reform Agenda payment steps, and the Commission has repeated the need for capacity in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports. The Commission's reform programme assessments also name these deficiencies, and without operating capacity the legal framework has little effect, so the issue is central to the theme. The rating does not rest on the volume of audit and action plan items.Validated
RI-TEC-023@MKDtractabilityLowProgress needs people the state has struggled to hire and keep (IT posts about half filled, 3 of 11 MKD-CIRT posts filled, a shortage the strategy says extends across the region), action across about 140 bodies, and budgets the strategy itself calls at risk, while the main infrastructure is at pre-feasibility stage and looks to outside funding. Past progress is weak, as most surveyed institutions had no response team five years after the previous strategy called for them, and the new 40% salary supplement is adopted with no item yet showing its effect. Strengthening MKD-CIRT alone would be more achievable than system-wide capacity, and the audit and strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.Validated
RI-TEC-024@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission has named the 5G toolbox in its recommendations in four successive reports (2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, two of these items being classified under the framework issue), and its November 2025 wording still asks the country to continue, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Legal steps did occur (2021 amendments, 2022 by-laws, the June 2025 law with supplier risk provisions), but the screening report says not all the 2021 amendments had been implemented. A reviewer could read the 2025 law as the start of improvement, but it began to apply only in June 2026 and no later EU item assesses it.Validated
RI-TEC-024@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe latest EU items ask the country to continue implementing the toolbox, including assessing suppliers and restricting high-risk ones, and the Reform Agenda requires the security by-law fully implemented by December 2027; the 2025 law is proposed as adopted, the by-law and supplier assessment as proposed, and the 2021 amendments as reversed because the new law replaces them, all of which are proposals for review. What remains is adopting and applying the by-law and actually carrying out supplier risk assessments and any restrictions, since the law gives the power (machine translated, capped at Medium) but no item shows it used. The Reform Agenda's statement that the step is largely achieved sits against its own partial compliance baseline and the Commission's later wording, and it appears to rest mainly on spectrum and legislation, so it is not treated as closure; the Commission's finding that this law's reform step was not achieved concerns the Code and the Gigabit Act and not the toolbox, and the law allows 15 months for by-laws, so the finding does not decide this gap.Validated
RI-TEC-024@MKDpriorityHighToolbox compliance is a Reform Agenda step and has been named in the Commission's key recommendations in four successive reports, and the enlargement communication presents it as a basis of secure digital infrastructure. The issue is narrow, one clause among several in the chapter's key recommendation, so centrality is the weakest part of this rating and a reviewer could reasonably set Medium. The small number of items did not lower the rating, as volume is not a criterion.Validated
RI-TEC-024@MKDtractabilityMediumFew actors are needed, mainly the regulator and the Ministry working with operators, the law already provides the power and by-laws under the 2021 amendments were reported adopted by the following year, which all favour progress. However, not all the 2021 amendments were implemented four years on, a supplier assessment planned from 2023 is not shown as done, and operators complained of having no consultation in 2021. The evidence does not show what restrictions would cost operators, so the rating is not set higher.Validated
RI-TEC-025@MKDdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Commission moved from 'yet to align' (2022) and 'further delayed' (2023) to treating the law as harmonised with the 2014 regulation and asking for the 2024 revision (2024), then to amendments transposing eIDAS 2.0, with 'some progress' for e-government and further efforts required (2025). Sources conflict on whether alignment with the 2014 regulation already existed in 2020 (screening report and 2023 strategy against the 2022 and 2023 reports), which affects the start point but not the trend. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive; the judgement rests on the issue's own items.Validated
RI-TEC-025@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe law was amended in June 2025 and the Commission counted the step as achieved for Reform Agenda purposes, while saying the law does not fully align and asking for further efforts in its 2025 report; the intervention statuses used here are themselves proposals. What remains is full alignment of the partially harmonised provisions, adoption of the 14 by-laws, which no item shows as adopted, and actual application. The machine-translated law text, capped at Medium confidence, says the amendments apply only from 1 June 2027.Validated
RI-TEC-025@MKDpriorityHighThe updated law is a Reform Agenda payment condition, and eIDAS alignment was raised by the Commission in each report from 2022 to 2025. It is the legal base of the electronic identification theme. The rating rests on these requirements and not on the number of items, most of which are provisions of one law.Validated
RI-TEC-025@MKDtractabilityHighThe remaining work is mainly legal drafting led by one ministry, with a gap analysis by SIGMA and a by-law roadmap already available, and the ministry met the June 2025 law deadline. Earlier delays in 2022 and 2023 and the staged by-laws, some tied to the wallet in December 2027, are the main limits.Validated
RI-TEC-026@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission said in 2024 that the tools were cumbersome and neither free nor user friendly, and in 2025 that they were still not, while its 2021 report recorded only a modest rise in electronic signature use. In 2026 it found the trusted list step not achieved despite the request of 30 October 2025, so steps were taken without a changed result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive, and the 2024 audit evidence that high-level eID did not raise use is machine translated and capped at Medium.Validated
RI-TEC-026@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedTwo providers offer advanced and qualified signature services, as the Commission reports and as the Reform Agenda step asks, but the same step is not achieved, the tools remain not free or user friendly, and the wallet and mutual recognition are still proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. The two sides conflict: North Macedonia reports the trusted list preparation complete and considers the step achieved, while the Commission says the self-assessment and published list are outstanding. What remains is inclusion in the trusted list (grace period to 31 December 2026), usable and free tools in common use, the wallet and cross-border recognition.Validated
RI-TEC-026@MKDpriorityHighJoining the trusted list and implementing the wallet are Reform Agenda steps, the first with a stated payment provision, and the Commission repeated its concern about the tools in 2024 and 2025. Recognition and use are central to the electronic identification theme.Validated
RI-TEC-026@MKDtractabilityMediumThe outstanding trusted list tasks are specific and technical, and two providers have passed ministry checks, which favours progress. Use and usability need many institutions and users, the wallet depends on regional partners and the mutual recognition agreement, and the list depends on Commission assessment. The audit found failed procurement of institutional seal certificates (machine translated, capped at Medium), which is a warning on delivery.Validated
RI-TEC-027@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission repeated the recommendation to align with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act in near-identical terms in 2023, 2024 and 2025, which sets the persistent default under the rules. The 2025 wording ('efforts need to continue') reports no result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-027@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe only responding intervention, alignment with the framework, has proposed status at the freeze, and this status is itself a proposal, so no aligned text is shown. Items are in tension and this is not recorded in the contradictions file: the 2023 screening says the framework is aligned with framework 2.0, while the 2023 report asks for alignment with the 2017 revision and the audit (machine translated, capped at Medium) found no study confirming alignment. What remains is a national framework shown to be aligned with the current European framework and with the Interoperable Europe Act.Validated
RI-TEC-027@MKDpriorityMediumThis is a repeated EU requirement across three reports, but no item places it in a benchmark, a Reform Agenda payment condition or the main findings list of a report. It supports the interoperability theme, yet the Commission itself treats use of the platform as the wider obstacle.Validated
RI-TEC-027@MKDtractabilityHighThe mechanism is legal and framework alignment, which one ministry can lead without depending on others. The caution is the record: the recommendation has not moved in three years and the plan is still only stated in a government strategy.Validated
RI-TEC-028@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentCommission wording that few institutions use the platform runs from 2020 through 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, which sets the persistent default; the 2025 report records only efforts and repeats the requirement. Connection and transaction figures rose (39 institutions in 2021 to 58 or 63 in 2025; 1.5 million transactions in 2022 to 8 million in 2024), and the Commission confirms the increases in 2023 and 2024, but the counts come from government documents, machine translated and capped at Medium, and most institutions remain outside. The 2020 Commission 'slight increase' and the audit's falling traffic are a noted difference of measure and period, and the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-028@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe platform operates and some institutions, such as customs, exchange data regularly, but the 2025 Commission recommendation still asks to complete data exchange and the responding upgrades and reforms are mainly proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. There is a confirmed contradiction: the country told the 2023 screening that the once-only principle is applied, while its 2024 Reform Agenda says institutions still do not gather evidence ex officio. What remains is regular use of the platform by the institutions obliged to use it, so that evidence is obtained ex officio as the law prescribes.Validated
RI-TEC-028@MKDpriorityHighData exchange and ex officio evidence sit in a Reform Agenda payment condition, and completing data exchange is a repeated recommendation on public administration reform in 2023, 2024 and 2025, in the main findings in the last two. It is central to the interoperability and data themes. The large number of items, mostly from one national audit, played no part in this rating.Validated
RI-TEC-028@MKDtractabilityMediumThe platform exists and the government controls it, and use has risen somewhat, which favours progress. Against that, the audit found about 1,300 obliged institutions with no costed plan, IT pay at less than half the private sector and no coordinating body, findings the 2025 strategy partly repeats (all machine translated, capped at Medium), and the Commission cites missing software and lack of will. ITU's account of a ministers' council is a noted difference over a different body, leaving how far coordination worked in practice uncertain.Validated
RI-TEC-029@MKDdirection_of_travelimprovingNCTS Phase 5 preparation started by 2021, delays were reported in 2023 and 2024, and the system launched in January 2025, with the Commission noting 'good progress' on IT systems in 2025. The Commission's recommendation to consolidate systems repeats each year, but the stated result changed. The sub-area wording matches this issue, yet the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-029@MKDunresolved_gappartly_addressedNCTS Phase 5 is live, but the 2025 screening rates alignment between low and partial, and Phase 6, the export system and ICS2 are proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is development of the remaining systems under the strategic plan, costed at about EUR 34.5 million, with full alignment planned for 2026 to 2030.Validated
RI-TEC-029@MKDpriorityHighE-customs steps appear in the Reform Agenda with a stated payment provision for Phase 6, and the customs IT recommendation recurs from 2021 to 2025, in the main findings in 2024 and 2025. The Commission calls alignment on accession critical to EU financial interests and security, so the issue is central to Chapter 29. Some Reform Agenda items carry a theme_doubtful flag because their wording stresses efficiency, not connection to the EU.Validated
RI-TEC-029@MKDtractabilityHighOne capable agency leads, and it has delivered NCTS Phase 5 after delay and kept Phase 4 running satisfactorily. The limits are IT staffing, the planned 15 experts not yet shown as hired, cost, and an EU-driven timetable to 2030.Validated
RI-TEC-030@MKDdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceThe requirements on ECRIS, the Visa Information System and Eurodac come essentially from one 2023 screening report, so there is no repeated or changed wording to compare. The 2021, 2022 and 2024 items concern a Frontex biometric plan and do not show whether readiness moved. The chapter scale was context only and not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-030@MKDunresolved_gapopenResponding interventions are proposed or lack a clear status, and these statuses are themselves proposals; part of the requirement falls due only at accession, and Eurodac access before accession has no legal basis, so 'open' does not by itself mean late. What remains is a functional criminal records system with ECRIS analysis done, the technical adaptations for the Visa Information System, an IT structure compatible with Eurodac on accession, and the funding for them.Validated
RI-TEC-030@MKDpriorityMediumThe systems matter for Chapter 24, but support is thin: one screening report states the requirements and no item shows a benchmark, Reform Agenda condition or repeated key recommendation. This is central with thin support.Validated
RI-TEC-030@MKDtractabilityLowProgress depends on the EU: the Commission says EU law gives candidates no Eurodac access, and the country reports it cannot build to Eurodac without the technical specifications and struggles to secure funding. The Frontex plan offers a route for border systems, but no item shows it being carried out.Validated
RI-TEC-032@MKDdirection_of_travelpersistentThe sectors do not share one trend, so this rests on those with repeated wording: CECIS from 2020 to 2025 (with 'no progress' in 2023), the business registers link from 2023 to 2025, and EU tax systems and own resources in 2024 and 2025. Some areas are better, including the 2021 COVID certificate alignment and food safety tools in 2025, which the residual label hides. The chapter scales were context only and not decisive.Validated
RI-TEC-032@MKDunresolved_gapopenThe latest Commission items still ask for the CECIS link, business register readiness, tax interoperability and the own resources system, and the responding interventions are nearly all proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. North Macedonia states it is technically ready for BRIS, but the Commission says machine-readable data alignment is still needed. What remains is connection to those systems, noting that BRIS and the Internal Market Information System also depend on EU decisions or accession.Validated
RI-TEC-032@MKDpriorityMediumEach requirement is repeated, and tax interoperability reaches the main findings in 2024 and 2025 and CECIS is an issue for immediate attention in 2024, but none is central to the theme as a whole and the only Reform Agenda references are railway and freight outputs in the government's text. This is a residual group spanning several chapters, so the rating is an average that would differ by sector.Validated
RI-TEC-032@MKDtractabilityMediumThe sectors differ: food safety shows active use of EU tools, the CECIS link looks technically limited yet has not been finished in over five years, and BRIS requires full company law alignment and access to groups open only to Member States and EEA countries. The rating is a mid-point, not a uniform finding.Validated

The extracted items give no data on what happened to EU workers in practice.Pending review

What closed the benchmark is not public, and there are no measured results yet, only an uncorroborated Government claim of improved procedures.Pending review
CMP-0003SRBRI-FMW-001Serbia reported in the 2015 screening report that its 2014 law contains a clause giving EU citizens free access on accession, and it later amended the law to simplify permits, but the Commission still says EU citizens are covered by the rules for third-country nationals. CMP-0004MDARI-TEC-028Moldova put a legal duty and sanctions behind MConnect from January 2021, and the operator reports high volumes, but no evidence shows that the sanctions were applied or what changed use. CMP-0005SRBRI-TEC-028Serbia has a 2016 legal duty to exchange data and a Bus to which the Commission says more databases are connected, but no source measures use by institutions. Around half of surveyed citizens still report being asked for documents the state holds.Pending review
CMP-0006MNERI-TEC-028Montenegro's register pairs in active exchange are reported as 18 and then 37 while institutions with access stay at 21, on government figures with no stated cause. CMP-0007MDARI-TEC-036Moldova digitalised services through a long donor-backed project and assisted access, and reports online use rising, with service-level data for 2022 showing most digital services unused. Limits and alpha lessons

Active limits

IDTypeLimit
LIM-0008countryNorth Macedonia (MKD) only; comparator evidence only for the 2 to 3 issues selected for run 1b
LIM-0009thematicRun 1 covers all of Chapter 2 (Freedom of movement for workers) plus the technology and AI theme: recommendations materially relating to the areas in taxonomy/themes.csv wherever they occur; incidental references to technology are out of scope; the full analytical chain is followed for every issue originating from an in-scope Chapter 2 item or technology and AI recommendation
LIM-0010thematicMaterial outside Chapter 2 and the technology and AI theme is out of scope unless it is needed to follow the analytical chain of an issue already in scope; there is no list of deferred chapters
LIM-0011timeEvidence from 2020-01-01 to the evidence freeze date; earlier material only by logged exception where needed to understand the origin or evolution of an in-scope issue
LIM-0012languageEnglish primary; Macedonian or Albanian only for core relevant sources with no suitable English version; each such source recorded in the register; machine translation flagged and capped at Medium confidence
LIM-0013analyticalNo interactive dashboard in run 1 (no country or thematic views); a single static read-only review page (index.html) surfaces validated material and labelled work in progress; outputs remain internal analyst products
LIM-0014evidenceNo National Programme for the Adoption of the Acquis (2020 or later) or its implementation reports: the Secretariat for European Affairs site had an expired TLS certificate and no copy was found elsewhere
LIM-0015evidenceNo official national material on the European Health Insurance Card or the electronic exchange of social security information (EESSI): the Health Insurance Fund site blocks automated access
LIM-0016accessibilityDocuments blocked by publishers for automated download are not retrieved manually in the alpha: SIGMA 2021 and 2024, OECD Competitiveness Outlook 2024 and Labour Migration 2022, UNDP Digital Readiness Assessment, IOM migration profile, two Metamorphosis monitoring reports, the 16th SA Council press statement, State Audit Office originals (ministry copies used)
LIM-0017evidenceResearch and civil society coverage of Chapter 2 is thin: one think tank study (MKD-RES-2023-001), evaluation highlights only (MKD-RES-2026-001) and one human rights report (MKD-CSO-2024-001)
LIM-0018languageAlmost all national government sources are in Macedonian only (some bilingual with Albanian); evidence on the country response will mostly rely on machine translation capped at Medium confidence
LIM-0019timeLogged exception to the time window: the 2015 Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners (MKD-GOV-2015-001) may be used only where needed to understand the 2021 and 2025 amendments (MKD-GOV-2021-001, MKD-GOV-2025-001)
LIM-0021timeClaims mainly about events before 2020 are kept only as controlled exceptions where needed to explain an in-scope issue; each is flagged out_of_window with the reason and listed for the analyst. Current claims that refer back to earlier events are in scope
LIM-0022thematicDigital skills are not part of the technology and AI theme; included only where directly linked to an in-scope technology or AI recommendation
LIM-0023thematicChapter 2 is read in its EU meaning: rights and access of EU and foreign workers in North Macedonia, labour-market access, equal treatment, EURES, the European Labour Authority, social security coordination, EHIC and anti-corruption measures tied to Chapter 2; emigration, brain drain and diaspora only where directly linked; nationals' access to EU labour markets and general labour-market policy out of scope
LIM-0024timeExtends the exception in LIM-0019 to Art. 5(2) point 1 of the 2015 Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners (MKD-GOV-2015-001), the only provision naming the EU, because a confirmed contradiction on quotas turns on it
LIM-0025evidenceAbout one in eight in-scope claims may be missed in EU sources, mostly of low importance (37 against 272 items in four sampled sources; the 8 of higher importance added). Long action plans and laws were screened by keyword and section, not read line by line
LIM-0026comparatorComparator evidence is gathered for three named issues only (RI-FMW-001, RI-TEC-028, RI-TEC-036), as a deliberate expansion approved at G6, with no full country model
LIM-0027timeLogged exception to the time window: comparator documents from 2007 onwards on RI-FMW-001 only, for Croatia, whose reform predates accession in 2013, and Serbia's screening report
LIM-0028accessibilityComparator evidence uses public sources only. Restricted EU documents are not used, including the EU common position on Montenegro Chapter 2 (AD 26/26), so what closed that benchmark is known only from public statements. Blocked sources, including the SIGMA 2024 reports, are recorded as gaps and not retrieved manually
LIM-0029languageComparator legal texts in Croatian, Serbian, Montenegrin or Romanian may be used where no English version exists; they are machine-translated and capped at Medium confidence

Alpha lessons

IDLessonStatus
ALN-0001Changing the pilot country from Serbia to North Macedonia before G0 required edits to about thirty files because country, chapter, dates, languages and examples were written into the codebooks, procedures and rules.implemented
ALN-0002A scope combining one chapter with a cross-cutting theme (technology and AI) could not be expressed with chapter and cluster fields alone, so theme tags planned for a later stage had to be brought forward.accepted
ALN-0003The helper tools depend on system software (text recognition with Macedonian and Albanian language data, PDF rendering) that was not installed in the working environment and was not recorded anywhere before stage 0.implemented
ALN-0004The rule that the freeze date falls just after the annual enlargement package did not match the date set at G0: the 2026 package had not appeared by the freeze date, so the newest annual report in the run is from 2025.accepted
ALN-0005A cross-cutting theme makes the whole of each annual report and the screening reports for all clusters relevant, so the EU source base is much larger than for a single chapter.accepted
ALN-0006Major publishers (OECD and SIGMA, UNDP, Council of Europe, some Council and national pages) block automated downloads, so several core sources need manual retrieval by the analyst.accepted
ALN-0007Almost all national government sources in scope are only in Macedonian (some also in Albanian), so most evidence on the country response will rest on machine translation capped at Medium confidence.accepted
ALN-0008Acquisition relied on an unversioned working script; three recording errors were caught and corrected, which shows the step needs a tested tool.accepted
ALN-0009Searching for sources with parallel agents, one per group of families, and checking every URL before download found 99 documents in under an hour.accepted
ALN-0010In the sample, the technology theme produced about two and a half times as many items as Chapter 2 (742 against 288), many of them sector IT systems of doubtful relevance, at about 6 to 7 hours of agent time for 11 sources.accepted
ALN-0011The quote check cannot verify quotes that cross a page break because printed page numbers and running headers sit between the pages, so sound items were shortened or dropped.accepted
ALN-0012Parallel extraction agents applied the same rules in different ways where the rules were silent (repeated text, sub-area progress wording, chapter basis), which makes counts and later judgements inconsistent.accepted
ALN-0013The automatic quote check confirms that a quote appears at its location but not that it is cut to the claim; three quotes that began too early passed it unnoticed until an agent re-read them.accepted
ALN-0014Applying analyst decisions R1 to R11 by revising the sample, rather than re-extracting it, took about half an hour per source and cut the sample from 1,054 to 732 items with every quote still verified; it also surfaced the next layer of boundary questions.accepted
ALN-0015The manual extraction check was reduced to simplified hand-coding of three passages and a stratified sample of 70 items, focused on missed and misclassified items, instead of reviewing every extracted item.accepted
ALN-0016Independent agents (a blind coder and reviewers who took no part in extraction) checked all 725 sample items in under 15 minutes elapsed, recorded verdicts before fixing, and gave usable error rates without analyst time.accepted
ALN-0017The main extraction weaknesses are missed neighbouring claims (about 14% of in-scope claims, mostly low or medium importance) and quotes that hold two claims; types and references are almost always right.accepted
ALN-0018The EU accession material says almost nothing specific about artificial intelligence (two EU requirement items in six years of reports); AI evidence for the country comes mainly from a national audit, so an AI focus cannot rest on EU requirements alone.accepted
ALN-0019Drafting the taxonomy in two parallel parts (Chapter 2 and technology) produced an overlapping issue on electronic exchange of social security data, because each drafter treated the shared items as its own.accepted
ALN-0020A draft theme issue with no supporting recommendation reached the G4 package, although procedure P2 requires one, because no tool tests this rule and the drafter only hinted at it in a note.accepted
ALN-0021Text conversion left pages with a heading over an image body almost empty, because text recognition only ran on near-empty pages; one regulator's full recommendations were missing until an extraction agent noticed.accepted
ALN-0022The second pass added 13.6% more items on non-EU sources but only 2.7% on EU sources, so the same check may have been applied unevenly.accepted
ALN-0023Two versions of one screening report were registered as separate sources because only exact file duplicates are detected; the same claims were counted twice until an independent check noticed matching sentences at stage 9.accepted
ALN-0024Independent agents checked random samples before the gate and found what routine validation could not: a wrong default for non-EU chain links, inconsistent twins, and the duplicated report. The analyst sees measured error rates rather than row lists.accepted
ALN-0025Working inputs for agents capped each intervention at 40 items, oldest first, which hid the newest evidence on the six most important laws and strategies until an agent reported it; they were judged again with full evidence.accepted
ALN-0026Parallel agents judged priority group by group and proposed 21 of 48 issues as High; a calibration across all issues gave 18 and exposed that the working test was stricter than the judgement rules, which moved a core acquis issue to Medium.accepted
ALN-0027The analyst became sole decision-maker for the alpha at G6, so no gate now needs a second approver. George gives review input, which reaches the analyst outside the gates.open
ALN-0028The first drafts of comparator cases contained 24 serious errors in about 480 claims, mostly claims of absence, values not following from reasons, and lessons going beyond the evidence. Routine validation and quote checks passed them all; only an independent read found them.open
ALN-0029Case inputs were filtered by issue tag, which hid relevant evidence tagged to a neighbouring issue, such as the Regional Cooperation Council's pre-filled forms scores, and led to wrong claims of absence.open
ALN-0030G2b passed under a standing instruction without row review, and only the later check found that key sources fell outside LIM-0029 as worded. Passing gates on instruction saved time but moved the discovery to the end of the pilot.open
ALN-0031Sources state few lessons, and transferability can attach only to an item, so the most useful material, the lessons drawn across a case, has no judgement behind it. The record does not fit what comparison produces.open
ALN-0032A rule in the coordinator's revision brief (no measure, no success judgement) was stricter than the judgement rules, removed the only two worked rows and went unnoticed until the recheck compared values with the disposition log. An instruction to helper agents had in effect changed the method.open
